title: AWQ: Activation-Aware Weight Quantization
hook: Not all weights are equal - protect the 1% that matter most (flagged by activation magnitude) and quantize the rest to 4-bit with minimal quality loss.
key_points: Identifies salient weights by looking at activation scales: weights paired with large activations matter more.
Protects those weights via per-channel scaling rather than mixed precision, keeping the kernel uniform.
Achieves near-FP16 quality at 4-bit weight quantization on a range of LLM benchmarks.
Complements GPTQ but uses activation statistics rather than Hessian-based second-order information.
content_html: Lin et al. proposed Activation-Aware Weight Quantization (AWQ) as a post-training method for compressing large language models to around 4 bits per weight. The core observation is that weight importance is not uniform: roughly 1% of weights connect to channels with large activation magnitudes, and quantizing those weights aggressively causes disproportionate quality degradation.
extra_html:
How it works

AWQ identifies salient weight channels by examining the scale of the corresponding input activations on a small calibration set. Rather than keeping those weights in a higher-bit format (which would complicate hardware kernels), AWQ applies a per-channel scaling transformation that effectively amplifies the salient channels before quantization and absorbs the inverse scale into the next layer. This is a math-equivalent reparameterization, so it requires no retraining and works with standard INT4 kernels.

Why it matters

AWQ produces 4-bit models that, according to the authors, closely match FP16 quality on language modeling and instruction-following benchmarks - with a smaller memory footprint than GPTQ at comparable bit widths. It is widely used in deployment frameworks like TinyChat and llm-awq. Read the paper on arXiv for benchmark details and the scaling analysis.

related.title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization
related.hook: Already trained a giant LLM? GPTQ squeezes its weights down to 3–4 bits afterward — no retraining — with surprisingly little quality loss.

related.title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Inference for Transformers
related.hook: Big transformers usually run in 16-bit. LLM.int8() halves that to 8-bit integers without losing accuracy — by treating a few rare 'outlier' features with care.

related.title: SmoothQuant: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for LLMs
related.hook: Activations are hard to quantize; weights are easy. SmoothQuant shifts that difficulty from activations into weights with a simple rescaling, enabling clean 8-bit inference.
